title: Refactoring Classic ASP
subtopics: Preserving existing behavior through regression tests
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of refactoring classic asp in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Improving names and formatting and Removing duplicated code.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study refactoring classic asp as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 110 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: Refactoring Classic ASP matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Legacy maintenance starts with understanding current behavior and dependencies before changing code. For 'Refactoring Classic ASP', create an inventory, define acceptance criteria, use version control, compare before/after behavior, test security rules and failure paths, and retain a rollback plan. Modernization should be incremental when appropriate and driven by compatibility, business risk, operational ownership, and measurable parity—not by framework fashion alone.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Improving names and formatting; Removing duplicated code; Extracting reusable procedures; Separating queries from markup; Improving error handling; Replacing fragile string concatenation; Preserving existing behavior through regression tests. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Refactoring Classic ASP
content_blocks.code:
<%
Function DisplayText(value)
  DisplayText = Server.HTMLEncode(CStr(value))
End Function
%>
content_blocks.expected_output: A single-purpose helper centralizes HTML text encoding for values used in HTML text contexts.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Keep helpers context-specific and add regression tests before replacing legacy behavior. Do not reuse HTML encoding as a universal sanitizer. The standard CodeLeaf browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; it does not execute Classic ASP, VBScript, ADO, IIS commands, PowerShell, or SQL. This block is therefore marked for static inspection unless you run it in the clearly identified local tool.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original sample and test data. Change one condition, input, provider setting, or runtime option at a time, then compare observed behavior with the expected result.
content_blocks.limitations: Not executed during course generation. Classic ASP examples require a configured Windows/IIS environment with the matching ASP scripting engine and any required COM/ADO providers. Provider-specific and IIS-version-specific behavior must be verified locally.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use a staging environment, written acceptance criteria, version-controlled changes, and a rollback plan. Record evidence instead of claiming a deployment or migration was tested if it was not. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of refactoring classic asp. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small, reviewable demonstration of refactoring classic asp using synthetic data. Include at least one of these syllabus concepts: Improving names and formatting. State the expected result first, then add one invalid or boundary case and explain how your program should behave.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

The syllabus coverage includes Improving names and formatting; Removing duplicated code; Extracting reusable procedures; Separating queries from markup; Improving error handling; Replacing fragile string concatenation; Preserving existing behavior through regression tests.
A reproducible legacy-code example records input, environment/version, expected outcome, observed outcome, and a meaningful failure case.
expected_output: A single-purpose helper centralizes HTML text encoding for values used in HTML text contexts.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
